newsitem.title: USA: General Mills Q2 volume aided by new cereals.
newsitem.headline: General Mills Q2 volume aided by new cereals.

text.p: General Mills Inc's cereal sales volume was stronger than expected in its fiscal second quarter thanks in part to new products that bolstered its U.S. market share.
Analysts, however, cautioned that some of those sales gains could be short-lived.

"I think part of this is the fact that they've had pipeline fill of new products (to retailers)," said BT Securities analyst John O'Neil. "New products tend to peak within a month or so -- ultimately that will taper off somewhat."

Earlier Thursday, General Mills reported its cereal sales for the quarter ended in November rose 10 percent from a year ago. Its market share in cereals was 25 percent versus 23.5 percent in the year-ago period.
Three new cereals, along with Frosted Cheerios introduced last year, accounted for 2.5 points of the market share, the company said.
Earnings for the quarter came in at $1.00 a share -- up from last year's $0.92 and above analysts' expectations. According to First Call, the consensus of analysts' estimates was $0.95 a share.
"The numbers look better than expected, clearly, from stronger than expected cereal volume," said Nomi Ghez, an analyst for Goldman Sachs.
Even if the market share from the new products slides, O'Neil said he expects General Mills' upcoming acquisition of Chex brand cereals from Ralcorp Holdings Inc to give volumes the next boost.
"They will tack on an additional three points as a result of that (Chex acquisition), and that will put them up in the 27 to 28 percent market share," O'Neil said.
Chris Jakubik, an analyst for SBC Warburg, however said General Mills' rise in market share was a temporary occurrence and a result of heavy promotional spending.

"Ultimately they (the cereal industry) have to face the fact that the category is not growing," Jakubik said. "Unless they can bring about some true product innovation which they have been talking about for the last two-plus years, we'll see increasing pressure to lower prices."
